findings.title: SQL injection in login via string-concatenated username
findings.detail: Source: request.form.get('username') (line 160). Sink: db.execute(query) (line 167) where query is built by string concatenation: "SELECT * FROM members WHERE username = '" + username + "'" (line 166). No parameterization. Auth bypass with username = admin'-- and full data extraction via UNION/boolean blind injection.
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query: db.execute("SELECT * FROM members WHERE username = ?", (username,)). Mirrors the safe pattern already used in current_user()/register().

findings.title: SQL injection in hive search via %-formatted LIKE clause
findings.detail: Source: request.args.get('q') (line 245). Sink: db.execute(...) (line 251) where the SQL is built with Python %-formatting: "... WHERE name LIKE '%%%s%%' OR location LIKE '%%%s%%'" % (q, q) (line 250). q is interpolated raw inside single-quoted LIKE literals; a quote in q breaks out and injects arbitrary SQL.
findings.recommendation: Parameterize: db.execute("SELECT * FROM hives WHERE name LIKE ? OR location LIKE ?", (f'%{q}%', f'%{q}%')).

findings.title: OS command injection in admin export-log via format param
findings.detail: Source: request.args.get('format', 'csv') (line 386). Sink: os.system("hivetrack-export --format " + fmt + " --output " + outfile) (line 388). fmt is concatenated into a shell command with no validation/escaping; outfile also embeds fmt. format=csv;id or format=$(id) executes arbitrary commands. Admin role is required but that only narrows the attacker set, not the injection.
findings.recommendation: Avoid the shell: subprocess.run(['hivetrack-export','--format',fmt,'--output',outfile]) and allowlist fmt against {csv,json,...}.

findings.title: OS command injection in queen registration (regex allows tainted hive_code into shell)
findings.detail: Multi-hop. Source: request.form.get('queen_tag') (line 535). The validator parse_queen_tag() uses re.match(r'^\d{4}-[A-Z]\d{3}-[A-Z0-9]+', raw_tag) (line 521-522) which is NOT anchored at the end (no $), so any suffix after a valid prefix passes. raw_tag.split('-', 2) (line 525) puts EVERYTHING after the second dash into hive_code, including spaces and shell metacharacters. Sink: subprocess.run(f'queen-registry --register {hive_code}', shell=True) (line 544-547). Tag '2024-Q001-AB; id' validates, hive_code='AB; id', executing arbitrary commands. Admin-only but still injectable.
findings.recommendation: Anchor the regex with $ and restrict hive_code to a strict charset; pass args as a list (shell=False): subprocess.run(['queen-registry','--register',hive_code]).

findings.title: Insecure deserialization of attacker-controlled request body (pickle.loads)
findings.detail: Source: request.get_data() (line 458) — raw HTTP body. Sink: pickle.loads(raw) (line 460). pickle deserialization of untrusted input yields RCE via __reduce__. Admin role is checked (line 453) but a compromised/CSRF'd admin session or any admin still gets full RCE; pickle on any external input is unsafe by design.
findings.recommendation: Do not unpickle request bodies. Use json.loads with a schema, or a safe serialization format.

findings.title: Server-side template injection in profile bio (render_template_string of concatenated input)
findings.detail:
Source: request.form.get('bio') (line 356). Sink: render_template_string(tmpl, ...) (line 362) where tmpl is built by concatenating user input into the template string: tmpl = "

...

" + bio + "

" (line 361). Jinja2 evaluates the bio as template source, so {{ 7*7 }} or {{ config }} / {{ self.__init__.__globals__ }} payloads execute server-side -> RCE / secret disclosure.
findings.recommendation:
Never concatenate user input into a template. Pass bio as a context variable into a fixed template: render_template_string('

Profile for {{ user.username }}

{{ bio }}

', user=user, bio=bio).

findings.title: Stored XSS via hive notes rendered with the |safe filter
findings.detail: Multi-hop. Source: request.form.get('note') (line 481) persisted via UPDATE hives SET notes (line 496). Sink: HIVE_DETAIL_TMPL renders {{ hive['notes']|safe }} (line 617), disabling Jinja autoescaping. Stored note content (e.g. <script>...) executes in any viewer's browser at /hive/<id> (view_hive has no ownership restriction, so notes are viewable cross-user -> stored XSS affecting other members).
findings.recommendation: Remove the |safe filter so Jinja autoescapes the notes; if limited HTML is needed, sanitize with a library (bleach) before storage/display.

findings.title: Path traversal in report upload (filename used unsanitized in save path)
findings.detail: Source: request.files.get('report').filename (line 306). Sink: os.path.join(UPLOAD_DIR, f.filename) then f.save(save_path) (line 312-313). allowed_file() (line 288-300) only checks the extension via rsplit('.',1)[1] and does NOT strip path separators, so a filename like '../../etc/cron.d/evil.txt' or '..\\app.py' passes the extension allowlist while os.path.join honors the traversal, writing/overwriting files outside UPLOAD_DIR.
findings.recommendation: Sanitize with werkzeug.utils.secure_filename(f.filename) before joining, and verify the resolved path stays within UPLOAD_DIR (os.path.realpath startswith check).

findings.title: Server-side request forgery in weather lookup
findings.detail: Source: request.args.get('location_url') (line 402). Sink: requests.get(location_url, timeout=5) (line 406) with no scheme/host validation; resp.text[:2000] is returned to the user (line 407). Attacker can fetch internal services / cloud metadata (http://169.254.169.254/...), file://, or internal hosts, with the response reflected back -> SSRF with data exfiltration.
findings.recommendation: Allowlist permitted weather hosts/schemes (https only), resolve and block private/link-local/loopback IP ranges, and disable redirects to internal targets.

findings.title: Open redirect via flawed is_safe_redirect allowlist
findings.detail: Source: request.args.get('to', '/') (line 439). Sink: redirect(target) (line 441) gated by is_safe_redirect (line 419-434). Two bypasses: (1) the relative-URL guard 'if not url.startswith("http")' (line 425) treats scheme-relative '//evil.com' and backslash variants as 'safe relative' and returns True, but browsers follow //evil.com to an external host; (2) the host check uses host.startswith(safe) (line 430), so 'http://hivetrack.example.com.attacker.com/' passes. Either yields an open redirect for phishing.
findings.recommendation: Parse with urllib.parse.urlparse, reject any target whose netloc is non-empty and not an exact match in the allowlist, and reject scheme-relative ('//') targets; for relative-only redirects require url.startswith('/') and not url.startswith('//').

findings.title: IDOR / missing ownership check in view_hive
findings.detail: view_hive(hive_id) (line 223-239) is @login_required but fetches the hive by id only: SELECT * FROM hives WHERE id = ? (line 229) with NO owner_id check, then returns its name, location, notes, harvests, and reports for ANY hive_id. Contrast with add_harvest (line 265-268) and add_note (line 489-492) which correctly add 'AND owner_id = ?'. Any authenticated member can enumerate and read every other member's hives, harvest data, notes, and report filenames.
findings.recommendation: Add the ownership predicate: SELECT * FROM hives WHERE id = ? AND owner_id = ? (and abort(403/404) on miss), consistent with the harvest/note routes.

findings.title: Hardcoded Flask secret key
findings.detail: app.secret_key = "hivetrack_s3cr3t_2024_DO_NOT_CHANGE" (line 30) is a hardcoded, source-committed signing key. Anyone with repo access can forge/tamper signed session cookies (set user_id/role=admin), defeating authentication and the admin role gates throughout the app.
findings.recommendation: Load the secret from an environment variable / secrets manager (os.environ['SECRET_KEY']) and generate a strong random value; never commit it.

findings.title: Weak password hashing (unsalted MD5)
findings.detail: hash_password() uses hashlib.md5(pw.encode()).hexdigest() (line 99) for stored credentials; verify_password compares the MD5 digest (line 102-103). MD5 is fast and unsalted, so stored password_hash values (members table) are trivially crackable via rainbow tables / brute force if the DB leaks.
findings.recommendation: Use a slow salted KDF: bcrypt/argon2/scrypt (e.g. werkzeug.security.generate_password_hash / check_password_hash).

limitations.impact: Static taint analysis of app.py only; no dynamic reproduction performed (reproduced=n/a).
